### In Praise of Windows

I woke this morning before my alarm, which is a rude way to begin any day, and lay for a minute watching the light move across the ceiling. It was not dramatic sunrise light, the kind poets are always borrowing. It was October light, thin and doubtful, coming through the east window of my apartment and falling in a pale rectangle across the opposite wall. A bus passed below. A neighbor's kettle whistled. Somewhere a pigeon rearranged itself on a ledge with great seriousness. I did not get up. I watched the rectangle slowly widen, and for no reason I can articulate, that felt like enough. A window does that. It gives you a reason to pause without demanding anything from you in return.

Human beings are strange about glass. For most of our history, we did not have it, or at least not in any quantity that mattered. The Romans made glass, but it was a luxury, and medieval houses were mostly dark boxes with shutters, oiled parchment, or thin sheets of mica if you were wealthy. To have a window was to invite cold, noise, theft, and weather into a life that had very few comforts to spare. In England, so committed were authorities to governing light that in 1696 they introduced a window tax, a levy assessed not on your house but on the number of openings that let in the sun. People bricked up windows to avoid paying it, and you can still walk through old streets in Bath or London and see those blind, ghostly rectangles on facades, windows that are there and not there. We have always wanted light, but we have wanted to control the price of it.

A window is a compromise made solid. A door says: you may enter. A wall says: you may not. A window says something more complicated: you may see, you may feel the air, you may imagine a different life, but you may not — at least not this way — come through. It frames the world and, in framing it, changes it. A tree seen from the inside is not just a tree. It is a picture that moves. A sky seen through a kitchen window while you are waiting for pasta water to boil becomes a small theater. Without the frame, it would be overwhelming or invisible. With it, it becomes bearable, beautiful, legible. Architects know this. They do not design windows only to let in light; they design them to edit reality.

That editing works both ways, which is why we are so ambivalent about them. We love to look out, and we are deeply uneasy about being looked into. Curiosity and privacy live on opposite sides of the same pane. Edward Hopper understood this perfectly. His solitary figures at night are almost always at windows, lit from within, exposed by the very light that was meant to make them feel safe. There is a melancholy in that: the window reveals you at the same moment it comforts you. It is why we pull the curtain at dusk without thinking, why we choose a seat on a train facing the landscape rather than facing it, why we feel a small, irrational jolt when someone on the sidewalk looks up at our apartment and holds eye contact for half a second too long. We want the view without the reciprocal gaze.

Painters loved windows because they were a ready-made metaphor for consciousness. Vermeer, in particular, could not leave them alone. In *Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window*, in *Woman at a Window*, in *The Love Letter*, the window is never just architecture. It is a source of light, yes, but also a source of thought. The woman is not looking at the street so much as she is looking inward, and the light falling across her face is coming from the same place as her attention. Three centuries later, we still put our desks near windows when we can, as if proximity to glass might make our thinking clearer. Maybe it does, not because the outside world is instructive, but because it gives the mind something else to do while it works — a drifting cloud, a swaying branch — a low-level distraction that paradoxically restores focus.

There is a special kind of looking that only happens from trains and airplanes. On a plane, the window is small, thick, and oddly meditative. You cannot open it. You cannot change the view. You can only watch the earth become abstract below you, fields turning into a patchwork, clouds into an ocean you are sailing above. People who claim not to care about views will still press their foreheads — disgustingly, but inevitably — to that plastic. On a train, the window is cinematic. It runs. It blurs foreground hedges and holds the distant hills steady. It makes travel contemplative rather than merely functional. It is, I think, no accident that so many songs, poems, and novels set a crucial revelation on a train. The window imposes a rhythm on your thoughts. You cannot rush it. You can only sit and let the world pass in its own order.

Then, of course, there is the other kind of window, the one we carry with us now. In the 1970s at Xerox PARC, researchers began using the word “window” for rectangles on a computer screen, and the metaphor stuck so completely that we now live most of our lives inside layered windows. We open a window to read, another to write, another to watch someone else reading and writing somewhere else. The metaphor is useful but also deceptive, because a real window does not refresh itself, does not track you, does not sell you the thing you were just thinking about. A real window is opaque to data. You can stare through it for an hour and it will not learn anything about you except perhaps that you are lonely. That uselessness is precisely its virtue. It offers a view without a feed.

Psychologists, inevitably, have studied what real windows do to us, and their findings are less poetic but no less interesting. In the 1980s, Roger Ulrich showed that hospital patients with a view of trees recovered faster and needed less pain medication than those who faced a brick wall. Light from windows regulates our circadian rhythms, tells our bodies when to be alert and when to sleep, and its absence is part of why winter can feel like a slow erasure. We are, in a literal sense, solar-powered animals who have built ourselves into boxes. A window is our compromise with the sun. To sit beside one for a long time is to be reminded, without words, that we are still connected to a larger cycle. We forget this until we are in a basement office or an interior room for a whole day, and feel a vague, unplaceable tiredness that is really just a lack of sky.

We close windows for as many reasons as we open them. Curtains, blinds, shutters, frosted glass, blackout fabric — an entire industry exists to modulate how much of the world we let in. In summer we close them against heat. In winter against cold. At night against strangers. At dawn, sometimes, against our own desire to be seen waking up. There is a ritual to it, especially in the evening. You walk from room to room, loosening the blinds, pulling the curtains together, and in doing so you perform a small daily act of ending. The house turns inward. The day, which had been spilling through every pane, is gathered up and put away. It is not fear exactly. It is a need for enclosure, for a space that is unambiguously yours, at least until morning when you will throw it all open again and let the street back in.

And opening them is its own ritual. The first warm day of spring, after months of sealed apartments, is almost unbearably moving. You push up the sash and the whole sensory world rushes back: exhaust and lilac, distant lawnmowers, someone’s radio, rain that has not yet fallen. As a child, the open window was a portal in both directions — you could lean out to shout to your friends, and you could breathe in the whole neighborhood at once. As an adult on a high floor, it is less practical and more symbolic. You are not going to climb out. You just want the air to change. That desire for changed air, I suspect, is why we complain so much about stuffy offices and airplane cabins. We are not really arguing about ventilation. We are arguing about feeling sealed in.

In churches and mosques and temples, windows were never meant to be clear. Stained glass turns light into story. The sun is filtered through ruby and cobalt and amber, and the room is bathed in a color that does not exist outside. It is a technology for making the divine visible, for reminding you that light can be transformed. Clear glass is modern, democratic, honest. Colored glass is older and more mysterious. When you stand inside on a sunny afternoon, the floor itself becomes a mosaic, and for a moment the building seems to be breathing color. No screen, however high its resolution, can do that. It cannot spill color across a stone floor and warm your feet.

Maybe that is the final lesson of windows. They teach us to pay attention to thresholds. We live surrounded by them — between inside and outside, private and public, light and dark, the life we have and the life we imagine having when we look out at the street and see other people living theirs. A window does not resolve any of those tensions. It simply makes them visible, framed, and for a little while, bearable. This morning, watching that pale rectangle widen across my ceiling, I was not solving anything. I was just, very briefly, looking through.
